title: Al-Kafirun: to you your way
hookLine: you have your way and I have mine (109:6)
carry: to you yours, to me mine

lines: A YEAR FOR YOURS, A YEAR FOR OURS.
cards: Let's split the difference. You come to my thing this week, I'll come to yours next week. In most of life, that's how peace gets made: a little give on both sides.
The leaders of Mecca, the commentators say, made the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ an offer like that. We'll worship your God for a year, and you worship our gods for a year. Everybody wins.
Everybody calms down. The answer was a surah of six lines, and its last line is still quoted today.

teach.b: The surah opens: say, O disbelievers. Kafirun means those who reject; here, the Meccan leaders who made the offer. Then it turns in a slow circle.
I don't worship what you worship. And you don't worship what I worship. And I won't worship what you worship.
And you won't worship what I worship. The repetition is the point: it closes the negotiation from every side.

teach.h: NOT NOW, NOT LATER, NOT IN TURNS.
teach.b: Not now, not later, not in turns. Then the last line, in Pickthall's translation: Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion. Scholars hold two things about that line.

First, it draws a clear boundary in worship. The Prophet would not mix his worship with theirs, even for peace; classical commentators read the surah as a declaration that worship isn't something you trade.
Second, the boundary is drawn without a threat. It doesn't say: and so we will make you. It says: yours is yours, mine is mine.

Some Muslims, especially today, read that line alongside another verse, in Surah al-Baqarah, that there is no compulsion in religion, as a basis for living honestly beside people who believe differently.
Scholars have discussed how far that second reading goes; it's a live conversation.
A hadith in Muslim says the Prophet recited this surah, with al-Ikhlas, in the two short prayers before the dawn prayer.

teach.h: TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.
teach.b: One says who God is. The other says clearly where you stand, and leaves others their own place.

how: Many Muslims recite al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in the two sunnah units of prayer before the dawn prayer, as the Prophet did, and some recite al-Kafirun before sleep.

o: people of other faiths living in peace
strangers from outside the tribe of Mecca
those who reject, here the leaders of Mecca

games.q: what's inside the surah — tap the pairs.
p: take turns worshipping, a year each
closes the deal from every side
unto you your religion, unto me mine

s: the surah accepts the offer to take turns
it refuses, four times over: worship isn't traded.
the last line comes with a threat
it draws a boundary and leaves it there: yours is yours, mine is mine.
the Prophet recited it before the dawn prayer
with al-Ikhlas, in the two short units before fajr (Muslim).

games.q: the leaders of Mecca offer a deal: a year of worship your way, then a year of ours. what is the answer?
o: refuse, and draw a line: to you your religion, and to me mine
games.why: the surah refuses the trade and ends without a threat: unto you your religion, and unto me my religion (109:6).

practice: Bring to mind one disagreement you carry, with someone whose view you really don't share, about faith, politics or how to live, and notice the urge to win it or to blur it.
Try a third thing: let it stand, and say to yourself, this is theirs, and this is mine. Hold your ground, and still wish them peace.

wordCard.voice: Al-Kafirun. The disbelievers, the name of Surah one hundred nine, which ends: to you your religion, and to me mine. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the disbelievers, from the root k-f-r; the surah's first address.

carryVoice: Your line: to you yours, to me mine. A boundary, drawn without a threat. One hundred sixty-five, in the books.
